title: "Errata"
subtitle: "On Coppock, Ekins and Kirby (2018), *Quarterly Journal of Political Science* 13(1)"
format:
  pdf:
    output-file: coppock_ekins_kirby_2018_errata.pdf
    geometry: margin=1.25in
    fontsize: 11pt
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
here::i_am("errata.qmd")

# Every number inside a corrected sentence below is computed here, from the deposited
# data, at the time this document is rendered. That includes the numbers that were not
# wrong: a token carried over from the published sentence is inherited on trust, and
# rendering the whole sentence from the pipeline is what verifies it.
out <- function(f) read_csv(here("maintained", "output", f), show_col_types = FALSE)

recontact <- out("text_recontact_rates.csv")
gaps <- out("text_reading_time_differences.csv")
t3 <- out("table_3_mturk_main_dv.csv")
t6 <- out("table_6_elite_main_dv.csv")
t7 <- out("table_7_elite_scale_dv.csv")

count_of <- function(label) {
  value <- recontact$value[recontact$claim == label]
  stopifnot(length(value) == 1)
  format(round(value), big.mark = ",")
}

on_target <- function(tbl) {
  filter(tbl, op_ed != "Constant", str_remove(op_ed, "^Op-ed: ") == dv)
}
off_target <- function(tbl) {
  filter(tbl, op_ed != "Constant", str_remove(op_ed, "^Op-ed: ") != dv)
}

# One decimal on the seconds scale throughout, and the article's own en dash for a minus
# sign, so a corrected sentence reads like the published one.
secs <- function(x) str_replace(sprintf("%.1f", x), "^-", "–")

oped_names <- c(amtrak = "Amtrak", paul = "flat tax", veterans = "veterans",
                wallstreet = "Wall Street")
gap_named <- gaps |>
  mutate(label = unname(oped_names[Z])) |>
  arrange(desc(mturk_minus_elite_seconds))
mean_gap <- mean(gaps$mturk_minus_elite_seconds)
reversed <- filter(gap_named, mturk_minus_elite_seconds < 0)

# The three elite main-DV effects the article names, and the strongest conventional
# threshold all three clear. The threshold is a comparison target rather than an input:
# nothing here is estimated from it.
named_elite <- on_target(t6) |> filter(dv %in% c("Amtrak", "Flat Tax", "Wall Street"))
thresholds <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1)
strongest <- min(thresholds[map_lgl(thresholds, \(p) all(named_elite$p.value < p))])
flat_tax_p <- named_elite$p.value[named_elite$dv == "Flat Tax"]

t7_off <- nrow(off_target(t7))
t7_total <- nrow(on_target(t7)) + t7_off
t3_off <- nrow(off_target(t3))
t3_total <- nrow(on_target(t3)) + t3_off
```

This note lists six corrections to "The Long-lasting Effects of Newspaper Op-Eds on Public Opinion," published in the *Quarterly Journal of Political Science* 13(1), doi [10.1561/100.00016112](https://doi.org/10.1561/100.00016112). **None of them changes a conclusion of the paper.** Every one is a sentence in the body text that disagrees with a table the same article prints, and in each case the table is right and the sentence is not. The tables themselves, and the findings they carry, are unaffected.

Every number in a corrected sentence below is computed from the deposited replication archive ([10.7910/DVN/3KBCJF](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3KBCJF)) at the time this document is rendered, including the numbers that were not wrong. The code and output supporting each correction are at [github.com/active-maintenance-aec/coppock_ekins_kirby_2018](https://github.com/active-maintenance-aec/coppock_ekins_kirby_2018).

**Bold marks what changed.** The first three entries are substantive: a comparison that reverses direction on one of four op-eds, a significance level overstated by an order of magnitude, and a miscount of the cells of a table. The last three are undercounted sample sizes, each of which the adjacent table gives correctly.

## 1. The elite sample did not read for 25 to 45 seconds less

> On average, our elite sample spent 25–45 seconds less time reading our treatment articles than the MTurk sample.

Corrected:

> On average, our elite sample spent **`r secs(mean_gap)`** seconds less time reading our treatment articles than the MTurk sample.

Across the four op-eds both samples saw, the elite deficit in trimmed mean reading time is `r secs(gap_named$mturk_minus_elite_seconds[1])` seconds on the `r gap_named$label[1]` piece, `r secs(gap_named$mturk_minus_elite_seconds[2])` seconds on the `r gap_named$label[2]` piece and `r secs(gap_named$mturk_minus_elite_seconds[3])` seconds on the `r gap_named$label[3]` piece, and on the `r reversed$label` piece the elite sample spent `r secs(abs(reversed$mturk_minus_elite_seconds))` seconds **more**, not less. The published range brackets the two arms the deposit's `opeds_compliance.R` computes, the Amtrak and flat tax pieces; the two it does not compute are the ones that break the range.

## 2. The elite main-effect significance level

> Turning first to main dependent variables, we found statistically significant treatment effects for three of the four treatments (Amtrak, Flat Tax, Wall Street) at p < 0.001, but did not for the Veterans op-ed treatment.

Corrected:

> Turning first to main dependent variables, we found statistically significant treatment effects for three of the four treatments (Amtrak, Flat Tax, Wall Street) at p < **`r format(strongest, scientific = FALSE)`**, but did not for the Veterans op-ed treatment.

The flat tax effect on its main dependent variable has p = `r sprintf("%.4f", flat_tax_p)`. Table 6 prints it as `0.411***` under a legend whose strongest level is p < 0.01, so the table and the sentence disagree about the same estimate. The Amtrak and Wall Street effects are significant at 0.001; the flat tax effect is not.

## 3. Table 7 has twelve non-target cells, not sixteen

> Of the 16 treatment effects on non-target issues, only one is statistically significant (Amtrak op-ed on Veterans outcome).

Corrected:

> Of the **`r t7_off`** treatment effects on non-target issues, only one is statistically significant (Amtrak op-ed on Veterans outcome).

Table 7 estimates four op-ed effects on each of four composite scales, so it holds `r t7_total` coefficients, of which four are on target and `r t7_off` are not. The parallel sentence about Table 3 counts correctly: five op-eds by five outcomes is `r t3_total` coefficients and `r t3_off` non-target ones.

## 4. The number of elite subjects who completed the survey

> This procedure yielded 2,169 subjects who completed our survey.

Corrected:

> This procedure yielded **`r count_of("Elite subjects enrolled")`** subjects who completed our survey.

Table 5, at the top of the same page, gives `r count_of("Elite subjects enrolled")` as its own total, and that is the number of rows in the deposited elite data. Tables 6 and 7 report the same figure as their N.

## 5. The number of elite subjects who responded in Wave 2

> As in the MTurk study, we asked subjects to participate in a follow-up survey after 10 days; after two reminders, we obtained 1,349 complete responses.

Corrected:

> As in the MTurk study, we asked subjects to participate in a follow-up survey after 10 days; after two reminders, we obtained **`r count_of("Elite responded in Wave 2")`** complete responses.

Table 5's Responded row totals `r count_of("Elite responded in Wave 2")`.

## 6. The number of subjects enrolled on Mechanical Turk

> We enrolled 3,567 subjects on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) in a three-wave panel survey.

Corrected:

> We enrolled **`r count_of("MTurk subjects enrolled")`** subjects on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) in a three-wave panel survey.

Table 1 gives `r count_of("MTurk subjects enrolled")` as its own total, and every column of Tables 3 and 4 reports the same figure as its N.
